title: Fake news: whose job is it to stop it?
titleDe: Fake News: Wer muss sie stoppen?

task.situation: ‘Open Question’, an online magazine for young readers, is holding an essay competition. This year’s question is: ‘Fake news: whose job is it to stop it?’ The best essays will be published on the magazine’s website, and you have decided to take part.
points: discuss the responsibility of online platforms and governments
evaluate the role schools can play in teaching media literacy
explain what individual users can do to stop the spread of false information

words.long: Give your essay a title. Write around 400 words.

task.de: Ein Essay für den Wettbewerb eines Online-Magazins: Wer ist dafür verantwortlich, Fake News zu stoppen? Drei Inhaltspunkte: Plattformen und Staat, die Rolle der Schule (Medienkompetenz), was einzelne Nutzer:innen tun können. Zuerst wählt ihr eure Position, der Titel kommt ganz zum Schluss.

focus.label: passive reporting structures
focus.note: Marked: impersonal reporting structures with a passive verb of saying or thinking: It is often claimed that …, It could be argued that …, X is said to …, X is thought to …, X has been shown to …, X is regarded as …. Other passive forms (… must be marked, … are held to account) are not marked.

gaps.q: In which other school subject could students learn to check sources? Not history. Give the English name, e.g. ‘ethics’ or ‘English’.
gaps.qDe: In welchem weiteren Fach (nicht Geschichte) könnte man lernen, Quellen zu prüfen? Nennt den englischen Namen, z. B. „ethics“ oder „English“.

steps.q: ‘Fake news: whose job is it to stop it?’ What is our position?
steps.de: Zuerst entscheidet ihr euch für eine Position, nach der sich das ganze Essay richtet.

options.label: Platforms and laws first
options.teaser: The main responsibility lies with the platforms, and governments must make sure that they act.

options.label: Education first
options.teaser: Rules are necessary, but critical users who have learnt to check sources are the best defence.

steps.q: Introduction: how do we introduce the topic and state our thesis?
steps.de: Die Einleitung führt in die Frage des Essays ein und endet mit unserer These. Prüft jede Option: Aufgabe, Aufbau, Wortschatz, Grammatik.
steps.own: Copy the frame. Then finish the introduction in your own words and end with a clear thesis statement.
steps.ownDe: Gerüst abschreiben, dann die Einleitung mit eigenen Worten fertigschreiben. Am Ende steht eure These.

options.label: Start with the dangers
options.text: Fake news is one of the greatest dangers of our time. False stories have damaged the reputations of innocent people, influenced elections and even put lives at risk during health crises. Many of them look exactly like real news, with professional headlines and invented quotes. This essay will therefore explain why fake news is so harmful and how readers can recognise it before it is too late.
options.reject: Off target: the question is WHO should stop fake news, but this thesis announces an essay on why fake news is harmful and how to recognise it. The thesis must answer the question in the title.
options.rejectDe: Am Thema vorbei: Gefragt ist, wer Fake News stoppen soll, nicht warum sie schaden. Die These muss die Frage der Aufgabe beantworten.

options.label: Start with a common claim

map.rules: {{Fake news, [[it is often claimed]], is simply the price of free speech online.}} In reality, false stories can now reach millions of people within hours, ruin reputations and even influence elections. {{Someone has to stop them, but who?}} {{This essay will argue that}} the main responsibility lies with platforms and with the governments that regulate them.
map.people: {{Fake news, [[it is often claimed]], is simply the price of free speech online.}} In reality, false stories can now reach millions of people within hours, ruin reputations and even influence elections. {{Someone has to stop them, but who?}} {{This essay will argue that}} rules help, but users who have learnt at school to check sources are the strongest defence.

options.why: Starts with a claim many readers have heard, then questions it and states the thesis.

options.label: Start with the speed of lies

map.rules: {{Never has it been so easy to spread a lie around the world.}} A single invented post can be shared thousands of times before anyone checks whether it is true. {{Responsibility for stopping such posts [[is usually thought to]] lie with}} platforms, governments, schools and users. {{This essay will argue that}} platforms and governments must take the lead.
map.people: {{Never has it been so easy to spread a lie around the world.}} A single invented post can be shared thousands of times before anyone checks whether it is true. {{Responsibility for stopping such posts [[is usually thought to]] lie with}} platforms, governments, schools and users. {{This essay will argue that}} schools and users, rather than laws, hold the key.

options.why: The inversion ‘Never has it been …’ makes a strong opening, and all four groups are named before the thesis.

steps.q: Body paragraph 1: what responsibility do platforms and governments have?
steps.de: Erster Inhaltspunkt: die Verantwortung von Plattformen und Staat, mit einem Beispiel und einer Bewertung. Prüft jede Option: Aufgabe, Aufbau, Wortschatz, Grammatik.
steps.own: Copy the frame. Then explain the problem in your own words, describe one measure against it and say how far it helps.
steps.ownDe: Gerüst abschreiben, dann das Problem mit eigenen Worten erklären, eine Maßnahme dagegen beschreiben und sagen, wie viel sie bringt.

options.label: What platforms decide

map.rules: {{Online platforms [[are widely considered to be]] the first line of defence against such stories,}} since their algorithms decide what users see. False stories [[have been shown to]] spread faster than accurate ones, partly because sensational content keeps people scrolling. {{Some platforms already work with independent fact-checkers,}} who add warnings to misleading posts, but a careful check takes days, while a rumour spreads in minutes. Corrections [[are also known to]] reach far fewer people than the original story. {{It is therefore reasonable to expect}} platforms to stop suspicious posts before they go viral, and governments must set clear deadlines and fine platforms that miss them.
map.people: {{Online platforms [[are widely considered to be]] the first line of defence against such stories,}} since their algorithms decide what users see. False stories [[have been shown to]] spread faster than accurate ones, partly because sensational content keeps people scrolling. {{Some platforms already work with independent fact-checkers,}} who add warnings to misleading posts, but a careful check takes days, while a rumour spreads in minutes. Corrections [[are also known to]] reach far fewer people than the original story. {{Laws can push platforms to act faster,}} but no filter can check every post, so readers must learn to do some of this checking themselves.

options.why: It explains why platforms carry responsibility, tests one measure and evaluates it in line with our position.

options.label: What governments can do

map.rules: {{Governments, first of all, [[are expected to]] set clear rules for online platforms.}} In the European Union, very large platforms have to assess the risks their services create, including the spread of disinformation. {{Such laws matter because}} companies rarely change a profitable business model unless they are forced to. {{The problem [[is predicted to]] grow with artificial intelligence,}} which can produce fake photos, videos and even voices in minutes. {{Recent European rules require}} such content to be clearly marked as artificial. Without obligations of this kind, even careful users would soon be unable to tell what is real.
map.people: {{Governments, first of all, [[are expected to]] set clear rules for online platforms.}} In the European Union, very large platforms have to assess the risks their services create, including the spread of disinformation. {{Such laws are necessary,}} but a state that bans ‘lies’ too eagerly may end up silencing its critics. {{The problem [[is predicted to]] grow with artificial intelligence,}} which can produce fake photos, videos and even voices in minutes. {{Recent European rules require}} such content to be marked as artificial. Such labels help, but technology changes so fast that users will always need the skills to question what they see.

options.why: Real European rules as examples, followed by an evaluation that fits our position.

options.label: Rules for platforms
options.text: Online platforms are said that they spread fake news faster than true stories because their algorithms prefer exciting posts. It is often claimed, that they earn money from every click, even when the news are false. For this reason, governments should set strict rules and fine platforms that do not remove such posts quickly. In the European Union, very large platforms already have to assess the risk of disinformation on their services. Fake photos and videos made with artificial intelligence must be marked as artificial as well. Rules like these are a first step, but they cannot solve the problem on their own.
options.reject: Three typical mistakes: ‘are said that they spread’ (→ are said to spread), the comma before ‘that’ (→ It is often claimed that …, no comma) and ‘the news are’ (news is singular → the news is).
options.rejectDe: Drei typische Fehler: „are said that they spread“ → „are said to spread“, kein Beistrich vor that, und news steht im Singular (the news is).

steps.q: Body paragraph 2: what role can schools play?
steps.de: Zweiter Inhaltspunkt: die Rolle der Schule beim Thema Medienkompetenz, mit Bewertung. Prüft jede Option: Aufgabe, Aufbau, Wortschatz, Grammatik.
steps.own: Copy the frame. Then evaluate the role of schools in your own words: what can lessons achieve, and how much can they do against fake news?
steps.ownDe: Gerüst abschreiben, dann die Rolle der Schule mit eigenen Worten bewerten: Was kann Unterricht leisten, und wie viel kann er gegen Fake News ausrichten?

options.label: Skills for life

map.rules: {{Beyond platforms and governments, schools [[are commonly thought to]] play a key role}} in teaching media literacy. Students can learn to check who is behind a website, compare sources and recognise manipulated images, for example in history or {SUBJECT} lessons. Analysing a viral post together in class shows them how headlines, photos and numbers are used to stir up emotions. {{Valuable as such lessons are,}} their effect only shows years later, when today’s students have become voters. In the meantime, the false stories that circulate now have to be stopped by those who control the platforms.
map.people: {{Beyond platforms and governments, schools [[are commonly thought to]] play a key role}} in teaching media literacy. Students can learn to check who is behind a website, compare sources and recognise manipulated images, for example in history or {SUBJECT} lessons. Analysing a viral post together in class shows them how headlines, photos and numbers are used to stir up emotions. {{Such lessons are worth every minute,}} as critical thinking protects people long after they have left school. Students who have once taken a manipulated post apart are far less likely to be taken in by the next one.

options.why: It names concrete skills and subjects, then evaluates what lessons can achieve, as the task asks.

options.label: Lessons and their limits
options.text: Teachers could show students how to check sources, for example in {SUBJECT} lessons. In other words, many adults have never learnt these skills at school. In contrast, students could also analyse viral posts in class and discuss why they spread so quickly. They could compare how different news sites report the same event and find out who is behind a website. It is widely believed that such lessons work best when they start early, and older students need regular practice because new tricks appear all the time.
options.reject: No topic sentence: the paragraph starts with an example. Two linkers do not fit either: ‘In other words’ restates the same idea, but adults who never learnt these skills are a new point, and analysing posts adds to checking sources instead of contrasting with it (‘In contrast’ → In addition).
options.rejectDe: Kein Topic Sentence, und zwei Linking words passen nicht: „In other words“ kündigt dieselbe Aussage in anderen Worten an, obwohl ein neuer Punkt folgt, und „In contrast“ steht, obwohl kein Gegensatz folgt.

options.label: An early start

map.rules: {{As for schools, Austria has taken a first step:}} since 2022, lower secondary students have had a compulsory subject on digital skills, which includes checking sources. Older students, [[it is often argued]], need further practice, for instance by analysing viral posts or comparing how different media report the same event. Such lessons give young people tools for life. {{Even the best lessons, however,}} cannot reach adults who left school long ago, and they work far too slowly to stop a rumour that is spreading today.
map.people: {{As for schools, Austria has taken a first step:}} since 2022, lower secondary students have had a compulsory subject on digital skills, which includes checking sources. Older students, [[it is often argued]], need further practice, for instance by analysing viral posts or comparing how different media report the same event. {{This early start is the right approach,}} as habits formed at school often last a lifetime. Students who learn to question a shocking headline at fourteen are unlikely to believe every post they see at forty.

options.why: A real Austrian example makes the evaluation concrete and shows what lessons can and cannot do.

steps.q: Body paragraph 3: what can individual users do, and how far does it help?
steps.de: Dritter Inhaltspunkt: was einzelne Nutzer:innen tun können, mit einem Argument der Gegenseite und unserer Antwort. Prüft jede Option: Aufgabe, Aufbau, Wortschatz, Grammatik.
steps.own: Copy the frame. Then explain what users can do, and answer the argument of the other side in your own words.
steps.ownDe: Gerüst abschreiben, dann erklären, was Nutzer:innen tun können, und das Argument der Gegenseite mit eigenen Worten beantworten.

options.label: Think before sharing
options.text: Individual users also have a part to play. Many false stories are shared by people who have read only the headline. How, then, is a single reader supposed to know which stories are true? Why should ordinary people do the work that platforms are paid to do? A short pause before sharing can slow a rumour down, and checking whether reliable news sites carry the story takes only a minute. Is that really too much to ask? Some argue that one user cannot change anything, yet millions of careful users together certainly can.
options.reject: Rhetorical questions belong in the introduction only. In a body paragraph they replace the argument: state the point instead.
options.rejectDe: Rhetorische Fragen gehören nur in die Einleitung. Im Hauptteil ersetzen sie das Argument: Formuliert den Punkt als Aussage.

options.label: A pause before sharing

map.rules: {{Individual users, too, are not powerless.}} Many false stories [[are believed to]] spread because people share them after reading only the headline. {{A short pause before sharing}} or a quick search for the original source can slow a rumour down. {{[[It could be argued that]]}} such habits would make strict rules for platforms unnecessary. {{This hope is unrealistic.}} Users would have to stay alert every single day, whereas one algorithm decides the news feeds of millions. Individual caution is a useful addition to clear rules, but it can never replace them.
map.people: {{Individual users, too, are not powerless.}} Many false stories [[are believed to]] spread because people share them after reading only the headline. {{A short pause before sharing}} or a quick search for the original source can slow a rumour down, and multiplied by millions of users, such habits achieve more than any filter. {{[[It could be argued that]]}} few adults will ever learn them, as many of those who share false stories left school long ago. {{This objection is only partly justified.}} Libraries and public broadcasters can reach older generations, and young people often pass their skills on to their parents and grandparents.

options.why: Two concrete habits, then an objection that is answered in line with our position.

options.label: Check like a professional

map.rules: {{Every user also carries a share of the responsibility.}} Before trusting a shocking story, readers can check whether reliable news sites carry it too, a method that fact-checkers [[are known to]] use themselves, and they can report posts that turn out to be false. {{Platforms, [[it is sometimes claimed]], are mere messengers,}} so the whole blame lies with the people who post and share. {{This image is misleading.}} A postman delivers letters without reading them, whereas a platform decides which posts to show, to whom and how often. {{A company that profits from attention}} cannot claim to be neutral about the content that attracts it.
map.people: {{Every user also carries a share of the responsibility.}} Before trusting a shocking story, readers can check whether reliable news sites carry it too, a method that fact-checkers [[are known to]] use themselves, and they can report posts that turn out to be false. {{Supporters of strict regulation insist that}} only laws can change the behaviour of large companies. {{There is some truth in this:}} fines [[are reported to have]] pushed platforms to remove illegal content faster. {{Yet laws are slow and end at national borders,}} whereas a critical reader is protected on every app, in every country and at no cost.

options.why: A practical method that anyone can use, then the other side’s view of users, answered in line with our position.

steps.q: Conclusion: how do we end the essay?
steps.de: Der Schluss greift die Frage der Einleitung und die drei Body-Absätze auf und rundet das Essay ab. Prüft jede Option: Aufgabe, Aufbau, Wortschatz, Grammatik.
steps.own: Copy the frame. Then sum up what the three body paragraphs showed and restate our position in your own words.
steps.ownDe: Gerüst abschreiben, dann zusammenfassen, was die drei Body-Absätze gezeigt haben, und unsere Position mit eigenen Worten wiederholen.

options.label: Sum up the position

map.rules: {{In conclusion, fake news [[is rightly said to be]] everyone’s problem,}} although not everyone has the same power to stop it. Lessons at school prepare future voters, and careful users can check a story before sharing it, but neither can control what millions of people see. {{Those with the most power carry the most responsibility:}} platforms must act before false stories spread, and governments must hold them to account.
map.people: {{In conclusion, fake news [[is rightly said to be]] everyone’s problem.}} Platforms can label misleading posts and governments can pass laws, but filters can be tricked and laws take years to change. {{In the end, the most reliable protection is}} a public that has learnt at school to check what it reads and that thinks twice before sharing a post.

options.why: It restates the thesis in new words and gives platforms, governments, schools and users their place.

options.label: Give a final judgement

map.rules: {{All things considered, the answer seems clear.}} Schools can teach young people to question what they read, and users can check a story before they share it. Yet they cannot keep up with a system that, [[it is widely agreed]], rewards whatever attracts attention. Responsibility has to start where the power lies. {{Only when governments hold platforms to account}} will false stories lose their reach.
map.people: {{All things considered, the answer seems clear.}} Platforms and governments must play their part, but no rule [[can be expected to]] foresee every new trick that appears online. Lessons at school and the habits of careful users, by contrast, adapt to whatever comes next. {{Only when users are taught to think critically}} will false stories lose their power.

options.why: The inversion ‘Only when … will …’ gives the essay a strong final sentence.

options.label: Look ahead
options.text: To sum up, platforms, governments, schools and users all have a part to play in the fight against fake news. Another serious problem, however, is that many young people now get their news from short videos instead of newspapers. Such videos rarely explain the background of a story. Newspapers should therefore offer free subscriptions to everyone under 25, so that young readers can get used to reliable journalism.
options.reject: A conclusion sums up; it does not open a new topic. Short videos and free newspaper subscriptions have not been discussed anywhere in the essay.
options.rejectDe: Ein Schluss fasst zusammen und bringt keine neuen Themen. Kurzvideos und Gratis-Abos kamen im Essay nicht vor.

steps.q: Now that the essay is finished, which title do we choose?
steps.de: Zuletzt wählen wir den Titel für unser Essay.
steps.own: Factual and to the point: the title names the topic and fits our position.
steps.ownDe: Sachlich: Der Titel nennt das Thema und passt zu unserer Position.

options.label: State the position

map.rules: Fake news: why platforms must take the lead
map.people: Fake news: why education matters most

options.why: A statement title tells the reader the topic and the position at once.

options.label: Ask the central question
options.text: Who should stop the spread of fake news?
options.reject: Wrong style for an essay: a question as the title sounds like a magazine article that wants to make readers curious. An essay title is factual: it names the topic in a statement and can hint at our position.
options.rejectDe: Falscher Stil für ein Essay: Eine Frage als Titel klingt nach einem Zeitschriftenartikel, der neugierig machen will. Ein Essay-Titel ist sachlich: Er nennt das Thema als Aussage und darf unsere Position andeuten.

options.label: Name the key idea

map.people: Critical readers: the best defence against fake news

options.why: Short and precise, and it already hints at the argument of the essay.

checks.en: A factual title that states the topic (a statement, not a question)
The introduction ends with a thesis statement that shows our position
All three content points: platforms and governments, schools, individual users
Every body paragraph starts with a topic sentence
Impersonal style (our focus): passive and ‘It is …’ instead of ‘I think’; no ‘you’, no contractions
The conclusion sums up our position without new arguments

teacher.aim: Die Klasse baut gemeinsam ein Essay nach SRDP-Standard zur Frage, wer für das Stoppen von Fake News verantwortlich ist: Plattformen, Staat, Schule oder einzelne Nutzer:innen. Fokus: Passive Reporting Structures (It is often claimed that …, X is said to …, X has been shown to …).
teacher.prep: A/B/C/D-Karten austeilen, eine Garnitur pro Person (ohne Karten: 1–4 Finger, die Tasten 1–4 wählen wie A–D). Beamer im Vollbild. Die Aufgabe am Beamer enthält alles Nötige. Im Gerüst-Modus den eingebauten Timer nutzen: 5–6 min pro Absatz.
teacher.heft: Neue Seite: Datum (rechts), „Essay“ als Überschrift, darunter 2 Zeilen für den Titel frei lassen (der Titel kommt zuletzt). Jeder Absatz beginnt nach einer Leerzeile, am Rand Intro, Body 1, Body 2, Body 3, Conclusion. Passive Reporting Structures grün unterstreichen.
teacher.flow: 7 Entscheidungen: Position, fünf Absätze (jede Entscheidung ein ganzer Absatz), Titel. Volltext (100 min, Doppelstunde): 4 min Aufgabe lesen und Position wählen, pro Absatz 2–3 min Abstimmung (mit Falle länger), Abschreiben insgesamt ca. 40 min, 2 min Titel, 5 min Checkliste, der Rest für die Besprechung der Fallen. Gerüst (100 min): 3 min Aufgabe und Position; pro Absatz 1–2 min Entscheidung, dann Gerüst abschreiben und eigenes Schreiben (Einleitung und Schluss je ca. 6 min, Body-Absätze je 8–10 min, weil sie ca. 95 Wörter lang sind), 1–2 min Vergleich mit dem Modell; am Ende 2 min Titel und 4 min Checkliste. Nach der Abstimmung die Fakten der gewählten Option kurz an die Tafel schreiben (nur bei Body 1 B: EU-Regeln für große Plattformen und KI-Inhalte; bei Body 2 C: Pflichtfach seit 2022/23), weil die Optionen danach verschwinden.
teacher.traps: Intro A (TA): Die These beantwortet eine andere Frage (warum Fake News schaden statt wer sie stoppen soll). Body 1 C (LSA): are said that they spread statt are said to spread, Beistrich vor that, the news are statt the news is. Body 2 B (CC): kein Topic Sentence, „In other words“ ohne Umformulierung (es folgt ein neuer Punkt), „In contrast“ ohne Gegensatz. Body 3 A (CC): rhetorische Fragen im Hauptteil; sie ersetzen das Argument, statt den Punkt als Aussage zu formulieren (rhetorische Fragen nur in der Einleitung). Conclusion C (CC): neues Thema (Kurzvideos, Zeitungsabos) im Schluss. Titel B (TA): Frage als Titel; das klingt nach einem Zeitschriftenartikel, ein Essay-Titel nennt das Thema sachlich als Aussage. Kürzel: TA = Erfüllung der Aufgabenstellung, CC = Kohärenz und Kohäsion, LSR = Spektrum sprachlicher Mittel, LSA = Sprachrichtigkeit.
teacher.notes: Das Essay hat fünf Absätze (Einleitung, drei Body-Absätze zu den drei Inhaltspunkten, Schluss). Jede Entscheidung ist ein ganzer Absatz: Einleitung und Schluss haben ca. 55–70 Wörter, die Body-Absätze ca. 85–105. Body 3 greift in den gültigen Optionen ein Argument der Gegenseite auf und beantwortet es. Keine echten Plattformen, Politiker:innen oder konkreten Falschmeldungen nennen; Beispiele bleiben allgemein. Die erste Entscheidung (Plattformen und Gesetze zuerst / Bildung zuerst) bestimmt These, Bewertungen und Schluss. Fakten im Text: In der EU müssen sehr große Plattformen nach dem Gesetz über digitale Dienste Risiken wie Desinformation bewerten. Seit dem Schuljahr 2022/23 ist Digitale Grundbildung Pflichtfach in der Sekundarstufe I. Studien zeigen, dass sich Falschmeldungen in sozialen Netzwerken schneller verbreiten als korrekte Meldungen und dass Richtigstellungen weniger Menschen erreichen. Nach der europäischen KI-Verordnung müssen Deepfakes als künstlich erzeugt gekennzeichnet werden. Wählt die Klasse in Body 2 Option A, ruft sie ein weiteres Schulfach auf Englisch (z. B. ethics, English, biology). Mit der Taste P werden die Passive Reporting Structures grün markiert; andere Passivformen sind nicht markiert. Differenzierung: Schnelle formen im Gerüst-Modus zwei eigene Sätze mit „be said to“ und „It is believed that“ um. Länge wie bei der SRDP: ca. 400 Wörter (360–440). Hausübung: zweite Fassung mit der anderen Position.
